summary: Opus-authored replacement copy for all twelve OPUS-REVIEW.json findings, numbered F1–F12 in review order (F1–F4 major, F5–F12 minor). Edits are limited to depth-2026-10-17/COPY.json opus.* plus four app sources (CryptographicDetail.jsx, DepthContent.jsx, App.jsx). No frozen evidence/contribution file or generated data is touched. F1: the proof explanation now separates (a) the two Groth16 public field elements carrying the statement digest, (b) the statement bytes, which sit on witness wires, are hashed by the in-circuit BLAKE2b gadget and are publicly rebuildable, and (c) remaining witness values, hidden only insofar as they are not reconstructible. The section heading is renamed accordingly and the prove stage no longer says 'private witness'. F2: assets are removed from the reuse list and explicitly qualified (asset declared in the program; predicate_digest coverage unread). F3: the unsupported other-key rejection sentence is replaced by a source-bounded statement that the claim-policy-key-to-vk_digest tie is not shown, and a matching open question is added. F4: the reclaim payer is removed, and genesis/Issue funding is no longer attributed; the open question now asks who funds fees, collateral, min-ADA and thread reserve. F5: the zero-ADA claim is replaced. F6: allocate is made conditional and key migration is marked proposed/absent in three places (circuit example, setup explanation, genesis stage). F7: 'Webs currently carry' becomes a design-scoped statement. F8: absolutes are made conditional on honest setup, knowledge soundness, collision resistance and gadget correspondence, with the forgeable recorded setup stated next to them. F9: ImplementationSummary renders all four status paragraphs with the absent-component list as a list. The list no longer denies the documented experimental mori-k2 CLI; it names the missing Web-level assembly/transaction interfaces and keeps Web consumer, real-context proofs, intent signatures, backing actions and reserve discharge. The setup drawer is retitled to state forgeability. F10: NotBound/TouchedOnly scope is explained in the walkthrough. F11: opening/genesis/post-expiry reclaim is distinguished from the absent reserve-return action. F12: the headline uses the concept's own positioning line instead of claiming proofs establish what a transaction does. No binding mechanism, payer, setup property or circuit property is invented. This is wording only, not security or prototype acceptance.

jsonPatches.expected: A Groth16 proof concerns one relation: a fixed system of arithmetic constraints that the compiler produces from one program action. Each value in that system sits on a wire. A few wires are public, and together they form the statement. All the other wires make up the witness. A proof convinces a verifier that the prover knows a witness that, combined with the given public inputs, satisfies every constraint. It reveals nothing else about the witness.
jsonPatches.replacement: A Groth16 proof concerns one relation: a fixed system of arithmetic constraints that the compiler produces from one program action. Each value in that system sits on a wire. A few wires are declared public inputs, and the verifier receives their values directly. Every other wire is a witness wire: the prover supplies it and the verifier never receives it. A proof is meant to convince a verifier that the prover knows witness values that, together with the given public inputs, satisfy every constraint. Zero-knowledge means the proof itself adds nothing further about the witness wires. It does not make a value secret when anyone can reconstruct it from public data. A value that is not a public input is therefore not automatically private.

jsonPatches.expected: Setup for the relation produces two public keys: a proving key and a verification key. The prover combines the proving key, the statement and the witness into a proof of exactly three group elements. That size stays the same however many constraints the relation has. The proof is bound to one relation's keys, so it has no meaning under the keys of any other relation.
jsonPatches.replacement: Setup for the relation produces two public keys: a proving key and a verification key. The prover combines the proving key, the public inputs and the witness into a proof of exactly three group elements. That size stays the same however many constraints the relation has. A proof is made for one relation's keys. Checking it under another relation's verification key provides no evidence about that other relation.

jsonPatches.expected: Verification takes the verification key, the public inputs and the three proof elements, and evaluates one pairing-product equation. Conceptually, the verifier first folds the public input values into a single group element using points fixed in the verification key. It then uses pairings, which let it compare products of values that stay hidden inside group elements, to check that the proof elements could only have come from a satisfying assignment for those public inputs. If the setup was honest and Groth16 knowledge soundness holds, a passing check means the prover knew a witness. In the Cardano design, this check runs inside the claim policy when a proof-claim output is issued, not again at settlement.
jsonPatches.replacement: Verification takes the verification key, the public inputs and the three proof elements, and evaluates one pairing-product equation. Conceptually, the verifier first folds the public input values into a single group element using points fixed in the verification key. It then uses pairings, which let it compare products of values that stay hidden inside group elements. The assurance is computational and conditional. If the setup was honest and Groth16 knowledge soundness holds, a passing check means that, except with negligible probability, the prover knew a satisfying witness for those public inputs. The recorded test setup does not meet the first condition, because its operator can forge proofs. In the Cardano design, this check runs inside the claim policy when a proof-claim output is issued, not again at settlement.

jsonPatches.expected: In a Web the compiled relation exposes two public inputs, and they carry a digest of the statement bytes the settling validator later rebuilds. Tying those two inputs to the actual statement bytes depends on two further things: the BLAKE2b hashing gadget inside the circuit and BLAKE2b collision resistance. Even then, the proof establishes only that the computation over those bytes was carried out correctly. It never establishes that the bytes describe the real ledger or a true observation from outside the chain.
jsonPatches.replacement: In a Web relation, the Groth16 public inputs are just two field elements. Together they carry a digest of the statement bytes that the settling validator later rebuilds. The statement bytes are not themselves public inputs. They sit on witness wires, and the circuit hashes them to that digest with a BLAKE2b gadget inside the circuit. Tying the two public inputs to particular statement bytes therefore rests on further assumptions. Among them are BLAKE2b collision resistance and the in-circuit gadget actually matching its specification. Correspondence between the compiled circuit, its verification key and that gadget has not been established. Even when those assumptions hold, the proof establishes only that the computation over those bytes was carried out correctly. It never establishes that the bytes describe the real ledger or a true observation from outside the chain.

jsonPatches.expected: Three kinds of assertion need to be kept apart. A concrete execution proof concerns one transition: this payment, fee and duty update follow from these statement values. A universal property certificate would concern every execution in a specified domain. An authenticated ledger claim concerns a fact reached through a named ledger-authentication path. Webs currently carry concrete execution proofs only. The other two are not established Strand kinds, and none of the three can stand in for another.
jsonPatches.replacement: Three kinds of assertion need to be kept apart. A concrete execution proof concerns one transition: this payment, fee and duty update follow from these statement values. A universal property certificate would concern every execution in a specified domain. An authenticated ledger claim concerns a fact reached through a named ledger-authentication path. In the current design, a Strand can only be a concrete execution proof. The other two are not established Strand kinds, and none of the three can stand in for another.

jsonPatches.expected: The statement names a single step. It identifies the state being spent, its sequence number, the settling script, the catalogue, the signed intents and the claimant, and it carries the body values the step computes over. The circuit hashes those statement bytes, and the resulting digest is what the two public inputs expose. The statement is public by design: anyone who sees the transaction can rebuild it.
jsonPatches.replacement: Three kinds of value need to be kept apart. First, the Groth16 public inputs: the two field elements that carry the statement digest. Second, the statement bytes. They describe a single step: the state being spent, its sequence number, the settling script, the catalogue, the signed intents, the claimant and the body values the step computes over. Inside the circuit these bytes are witness bits, which the circuit hashes to the digest. Outside the circuit they are public in practice, because the settling validator and any observer can rebuild them from the transaction and the state it spends. Sitting on a witness wire does not make them private. Third, the remaining witness values, described below.

jsonPatches.expected: Inside the reviewed relation source, some header fields are compiled constants: the tag, the family, predicate_digest, shape_digest and body_len. The context fields from vk_digest through intents_digest, including claimant_vkh, are free witness bits. The circuit hashes these bits into the statement but does not interpret them. As a result, the circuit commits to whatever context it is given without checking it. Comparing that context with the real transaction is the consuming validator's job, not the circuit's.
jsonPatches.replacement: Inside the reviewed relation source, some header fields are compiled constants: the tag, the family, predicate_digest, shape_digest and body_len. The context fields from vk_digest through intents_digest, including claimant_vkh, are free witness bits. The circuit hashes these bits into the statement digest but does not interpret them, so it accepts whatever context it is given without checking it. These fields remain part of the publicly rebuildable statement bytes. Calling them witness bits describes how the circuit receives them, not secrecy. Comparing that context with the real transaction is the consuming validator's job, not the circuit's.

jsonPatches.expected: The witness is every other value that satisfies the constraints, and it stays with the prover. Zero-knowledge protects the witness, but it does not make a transition private. The statement, the proof-claim outputs, the settlement transaction and its actual outputs are all visible on the ledger. Public evidence bundles leave out witness values, private keys and setup secrets.
jsonPatches.replacement: The remaining witness values are whatever else the prover supplies to satisfy the constraints. Zero-knowledge keeps them out of the proof. They stay hidden only to the extent that they cannot be reconstructed from public data, and zero-knowledge does not make a transition private. The statement bytes, the proof-claim outputs, the settlement transaction and its actual outputs are all visible on the ledger. Public evidence bundles leave out witness values, private keys and setup secrets.

jsonPatches.expected: On Cardano, a Web catalogue fixes its verification-key digests at genesis and carries them unchanged. Replacing a key therefore requires a key-migration action that carries any remaining duties forward. Revoking an intent advances the sequence number but does not migrate keys.
jsonPatches.replacement: On Cardano, the reviewed source fixes a Web catalogue's verification-key digests at genesis and carries them unchanged. Replacing a key would therefore need a key-migration action that carries any remaining duties forward. That action is a proposal and does not exist in the reviewed source. Revoking an intent advances the sequence number but does not migrate keys.

jsonPatches.expected: The unit for counting setups is the distinct compiled relation, including any additional Groth16 wrapper circuit. The count does not depend on how many transactions, wallets, users, claims, assets or logical properties exist on Cardano. New transactions, users, assets and public-input values inside an unchanged compiled relation all reuse its keys. Aggregating proofs does not remove the setups that the underlying circuits need.
jsonPatches.replacement: The unit for counting setups is the distinct compiled relation, including any additional Groth16 wrapper circuit. The number of transactions, wallets, users or claims on Cardano does not set the count, and counts of logical properties or review identifiers do not determine it. New transactions, users and public-input values inside an unchanged compiled relation reuse its keys. Assets are a different case in the current source. The invoice program declares its CASH asset as a literal, so a different asset may mean a different program, a different predicate identity and therefore a different circuit. Whether it does depends on exactly which fields predicate_digest covers, and the source file that defines that coverage was not read. Aggregating proofs does not remove the setups that the underlying circuits need.

jsonPatches.expected: Now take a 35 CASH partial payment on one escrow and a different partial payment on another escrow, with another claimant and another sequence number. Both use the same relation and the same keys, because only free context and body values differ. Their statements differ, so their digests differ. A proof made for one step therefore does not match the statement the validator rebuilds for the other.
jsonPatches.replacement: Now take a 35 CASH partial payment on one escrow and a different partial payment on another escrow, with another claimant and another sequence number. Both use the same relation and the same keys, because only free context and body values differ. Their statements differ, so under BLAKE2b collision resistance their digests differ except with negligible probability. A claim made for one step therefore does not match the statement the validator rebuilds for the other.

jsonPatches.expected: The conditional-reserve allocate action is a different program action with a different predicate identity. Its predicate_digest constant differs, which makes it a distinct circuit with its own phase 2. It can still share a phase 1 with the invoice relation if the curve, format and capacity are compatible. Changing a bound or the public-input layout of the invoice relation itself also produces a new circuit and a new verification-key digest. Because catalogues are fixed at genesis, putting that new key into use requires a key-migration action.
jsonPatches.replacement: The conditional-reserve allocate action belongs to a different program. No compiled relation for it is supplied. If it were compiled under the current path with a different predicate_digest constant, it would be a distinct circuit with its own phase 2. It could still share a phase 1 with the invoice relation if the curve, format and capacity are compatible. Changing a bound or the public-input layout of the invoice relation itself also produces a new circuit and a new verification-key digest. In the reviewed source, catalogues are fixed at genesis, so putting that new key into use would need a key-migration action. That action is a proposal; the reviewed source has no key migration.

jsonPatches.expected: vk_digest is the first of the context fields hashed into the statement. The catalogue fixes its verification-key digests at genesis, and owner intents sign the target VK digest. A claim issued under another key does not match the statement the validator rebuilds from the catalogue. Whether a given verification key matches its compiled constraint matrices is not established.
jsonPatches.replacement: vk_digest is the first of the context fields hashed into the statement. Like the other context fields, it is a free witness value that the circuit hashes but does not interpret. In the reviewed source, the catalogue fixes its verification-key digests at genesis, and owner intents sign the target VK digest. The supplied sources do not show how the claim policy ties the verification key it checks a proof under to the vk_digest field. This page therefore does not claim that a proof checked under some other key is refused. Whether a given verification key matches its compiled constraint matrices is also not established.
